{{Short description|Formulation of classical mechanics}}
{{classical mechanics|formulations}}
{{calculus|expanded=specialized}}
In [[physics]], the '''Hamilton–Jacobi equation''', named after [[William Rowan Hamilton]] and [[Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi]], is an alternative formulation of [[classical mechanics]], equivalent to other formulations such as [[Newton's laws of motion]], [[Lagrangian mechanics]] and [[Hamiltonian mechanics]].

The Hamilton–Jacobi equation is a formulation of mechanics in which the motion of a particle can be represented as a wave.  In this sense, it fulfilled a long-held goal of theoretical physics (dating at least to [[Johann Bernoulli]] in the eighteenth century) of finding an analogy between the propagation of light and the motion of a particle.  The wave equation followed by mechanical systems is similar to, but not identical with, the [[Schrödinger equation]], as described below; for this reason, the Hamilton–Jacobi equation is considered the "closest approach" of [[classical mechanics]] to [[quantum mechanics]].<ref name=Goldstein_484>{{cite book |last=Goldstein |first=Herbert |author-link=Herbert Goldstein |year=1980 |title= Classical Mechanics |edition=2nd |publisher=Addison-Wesley |location=Reading, MA |isbn= 978-0-201-02918-5 |pages=484–492|title-link=Classical Mechanics (Goldstein) }} (particularly the discussion beginning in the last paragraph of page 491)</ref><ref name=Sakurai_103>{{cite book |last=Sakurai |first=J. J. |author-link=J. J. Sakurai |year=1994 |title= Modern Quantum Mechanics |edition=rev. |publisher=Addison-Wesley |location=Reading, MA |isbn= 0-201-53929-2 |pages=103–107|title-link=Modern Quantum Mechanics }}</ref> The qualitative form of this connection is called [[Hamilton's optico-mechanical analogy]].

In mathematics, the Hamilton–Jacobi equation is a [[Necessity and sufficiency#Necessity|necessary condition]] describing extremal [[geometry]] in generalizations of problems from the [[calculus of variations]]. It can be understood as a special case of the [[Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation]] from [[dynamic programming]].<ref>{{cite book |first=Rudolf E. |last=Kálmán |chapter=The Theory of Optimal Control and the Calculus of Variations |title=Mathematical Optimization Techniques |editor-first=Richard |editor-last=Bellman |location=Berkeley |publisher=University of California Press |year=1963 |pages=309–331 |oclc=1033974 }}</ref>

== Overview ==
The Hamilton–Jacobi equation is a first-order, [[non-linear differential equation|non-linear]] [[partial differential equation]]

{{Equation box 1
|equation = <math> - \frac{\partial S}{\partial t} = H{\left(\mathbf{q},\frac{\partial S}{\partial \mathbf{q}},t \right)}.</math>
|2=border|border colour = #50C878
|background colour = #ECFCF4|title=}}

for a system of particles at coordinates {{tmath|1= \mathbf{q} }}. The function <math>H</math> is the system's [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian]] giving the system's energy. The solution of this equation is the [[action (physics)|''action'']], {{tmath|1= S }}, called ''Hamilton's principal function''.<ref>{{cite book |first1=L.N. |last1=Hand |first2=J.D. |last2=Finch |title=Analytical Mechanics |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-521-57572-0 }}</ref>{{rp|291|q=The solution S ... is called Hamilton's Principal Function}} 
The solution can be related to the system Lagrangian <math>\ \mathcal{L}\ </math> by an indefinite integral of the form used in the [[principle of least action]]:<ref name=Goldstein3/>{{rp|431}}
<math display="block">\ S = \int \mathcal{L}\ \mathrm{d}t + ~\mathsf{ some\ constant}~</math>
Geometrical surfaces of constant action are perpendicular to system trajectories, creating a wavefront-like view of the system dynamics. This property of the Hamilton–Jacobi equation connects classical mechanics to quantum mechanics.<ref name=Coopersmith2017>{{cite book |last=Coopersmith |first=Jennifer |year=2017 |title=The lazy universe: an introduction to the principle of least action |place=Oxford, UK / New York, NY |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-874304-0 |url=http://archive.org/details/lazyuniverseintr0000coop }}</ref>{{rp|175}}

== Mathematical formulation ==
=== Notation ===
Boldface variables such as <math>\mathbf{q}</math> represent a list of <math>N</math> [[generalized coordinates]],
<math display="block">\mathbf{q} = (q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_{N-1}, q_N)</math>

A dot over a variable or list signifies the time derivative (see [[Newton's notation]]). For example,
<math display="block">\dot{\mathbf{q}} = \frac{d\mathbf{q}}{dt}.</math>

The [[dot product]] notation between two lists of the same number of coordinates is a shorthand for the sum of the products of corresponding components, such as
<math display="block">\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{q} = \sum_{k=1}^N p_k q_k.</math>

=== The action functional (a.k.a. Hamilton's principal function) ===
{{anchor|Hamilton's principal function}}

==== Definition ====
Let the [[Hessian matrix]] <math display="inline">H_\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{\dot q},t) = \left\{\partial^2 \mathcal{L}/\partial {\dot q}^i\partial {\dot q}^j\right\}_{ij}</math> be invertible. The relation
<math display="block">
\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial{\dot q}^i} =
\sum^n_{j=1}\left(\frac{\partial^2 \mathcal{L}}{\partial{\dot q}^i\partial{\dot q}^j} {\ddot q}^j
+ \frac{\partial^2 \mathcal{L}}{\partial{\dot q}^i\partial{q}^j}{\dot q}^j \right)
+\frac{\partial^2 \mathcal{L}}{\partial{\dot q}^i \partial t},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,
</math>
shows that the [[Euler–Lagrange equations]] form a <math>n \times n</math> system of second-order ordinary differential equations. Inverting the matrix <math>H_\mathcal{L}</math> transforms this system into
<math display="block">\ddot q^i = F_i(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{\dot q},t),\ i=1,\ldots, n.</math>

Let a time instant <math>t_0</math> and a point <math>\mathbf{q}_0 \in M</math> in the configuration space be fixed. The existence and uniqueness theorems guarantee that, for every <math>\mathbf{v}_0,</math> the [[initial value problem]] with the conditions <math>\gamma|_{\tau=t_0} = \mathbf{q}_0</math> and <math>{\dot \gamma}|_{\tau=t_0} = \mathbf{v}_0</math> has a locally unique solution <math>\gamma = \gamma(\tau; t_0,\mathbf{q}_0,\mathbf{v}_0).</math> Additionally, let there be a sufficiently small time interval <math> (t_0,t_1) </math> such that extremals with different initial velocities <math>\mathbf{v}_0</math> would not intersect in <math>M \times (t_0,t_1).</math> The latter means that, for any <math>\mathbf{q} \in M</math> and any <math>t \in (t_0,t_1),</math> there can be at most one extremal <math>\gamma=\gamma(\tau;t,t_0,\mathbf{q},\mathbf{q}_0)</math> for which <math>\gamma|_{\tau=t_0} = \mathbf{q}_0</math> and <math>\gamma|_{\tau=t} = \mathbf{q}.</math> Substituting <math>\gamma=\gamma(\tau;t,t_0,\mathbf{q},\mathbf{q}_0)</math> into the [[action (physics)|action]] functional results in the Hamilton's principal function (HPF)

{{Equation box 1
|equation = <math>
S(\mathbf{q},t;\mathbf{q}_0,t_0) \ \stackrel{\text{def}}{=} \int^t_{t_0} \mathcal{L}(\gamma(\tau;\cdot),\dot\gamma(\tau;\cdot),\tau)\,d\tau,</math>
|2=border|border colour = #50C878
|background colour = #ECFCF4}}
where
* <math>\gamma=\gamma(\tau;t,t_0,\mathbf{q},\mathbf{q}_0),</math>
* <math>\gamma|_{\tau=t_0} = \mathbf{q}_0,</math>
* <math>\gamma|_{\tau=t} = \mathbf{q}.</math>

=== Formula for the momenta ===
The [[momentum|momenta]] are defined as the quantities <math display="inline"> p_i(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{\dot q},t) = \partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \dot q^i.</math> This section shows that the dependency of <math>p_i</math> on <math>\mathbf{\dot q}</math> disappears, once the HPF is known.

Indeed, let a time instant <math>t_0</math> and a point <math>\mathbf{q}_0</math> in the configuration space be fixed. For every time instant <math>t</math> and a point <math>\mathbf{q},</math> let <math>\gamma=\gamma(\tau;t,t_0,\mathbf{q},\mathbf{q}_0)</math> be the (unique) extremal from the definition of the Hamilton's principal function {{tmath|1= S }}. Call <math>\mathbf{v}\, \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\, \dot \gamma(\tau;t,t_0,\mathbf{q},\mathbf{q}_0)|_{\tau=t}</math> the velocity at {{tmath|1= \tau = t }}. Then
{{Equation box 1
|equation = <math>\frac{\partial S}{\partial q^i} = \left.\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot q^i}\right|_{\mathbf{\dot q} = \mathbf{v}}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!, \quad i=1,\ldots,n.</math>
|title=}}

{{math proof|proof=
While the proof below assumes the configuration space to be an open subset of <math>\R^n,</math> the underlying technique applies equally to arbitrary [[smooth manifolds|spaces]]. In the context of this proof, the calligraphic letter <math>\mathcal{S}</math> denotes the action functional, and the italic <math>S</math> the Hamilton's principal function.

'''Step 1.''' Let <math>\xi = \xi(t)</math> be a path in the configuration space, and <math>\delta \xi = \delta \xi(t)</math> a vector field along <math>\xi</math>. (For each <math>t,</math> the vector <math>\delta\xi(t)</math> is called ''perturbation'', ''infinitesimal variation'' or ''[[virtual displacement]]'' of the mechanical system at the point <math>\xi(t)</math>). Recall that the [[Gateaux derivative|variation]] <math>\delta \mathcal{S}_{\delta \xi}[\gamma,t_1,t_0]</math> of the action <math>\mathcal{S}</math> at the point <math>\xi</math> in the direction <math>\delta \xi</math> is given by the formula
<math display="block">
\delta \mathcal{S}_{\delta \xi}[\xi,t_1,t_0] = \int^{t_1}_{t_0} \left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{q}} - \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{\dot q}}\right)\delta \xi\,dt + \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{\dot q}}\,\delta \xi\Biggl|^{t_1}_{t_0},
</math>
where one should substitute <math>q^i=\xi^i(t)</math> and <math>\dot q^i = \dot \xi^i(t)</math> after calculating the partial derivatives on the right-hand side. (This formula follows from the definition of Gateaux derivative via integration by parts).

Assume that <math>\xi</math> is an extremal. Since <math>\xi</math> now satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equations, the integral term vanishes. If <math>\xi</math>'s starting point <math>\mathbf{q}_0</math> is fixed, then, by the same logic that was used to derive the Euler–Lagrange equations, <math>\delta \xi(t_0) = 0.</math> Thus,
<math display="block">
\delta\mathcal{S}_{\delta \xi}[\xi,t;t_0]
= \left. \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{\dot q}} \right|^{\mathbf{q}=\xi(t)}_{\mathbf{\dot q}
= \dot \xi(t)}\, \delta \xi(t).
</math>

'''Step 2.''' Let <math>\gamma=\gamma(\tau;\mathbf{q},\mathbf{q}_0,t,t_0)</math> be the (unique) extremal from the definition of HPF, <math>\delta\gamma = \delta\gamma(\tau)</math> a vector field along <math>\gamma,</math> and <math>\gamma_\varepsilon=\gamma_\varepsilon(\tau;\mathbf{q}_\varepsilon,\mathbf{q}_0,t,t_0)</math> a variation of <math>\gamma</math> "compatible" with <math>\delta \gamma.</math> In precise terms, <math>\gamma_\varepsilon|_{\varepsilon = 0} = \gamma,</math>
<math>\dot\gamma_\varepsilon|_{\varepsilon = 0} = \delta\gamma,</math> <math>\gamma_\varepsilon|_{\tau=t_0} = \gamma|_{\tau=t_0} = \mathbf{q}_0.</math>

By definition of HPF and Gateaux derivative,
<math display="block">
\delta\mathcal{S}_{\delta \gamma}[\gamma,t]
\overset{\text{def}}{{}={}} \left. \frac{d\mathcal{S}[\gamma_\varepsilon,t]}{d\varepsilon} \right|_{\varepsilon=0}
= \left. \frac{dS(\gamma_\varepsilon(t),t)}{d\varepsilon} \right|_{\varepsilon=0}
= \frac{\partial S}{\mathbf{\partial q}} \, \delta\gamma(t).
</math>

Here, we took into account that <math>\mathbf{q}=\gamma(t;\mathbf{q},\mathbf{q}_0,t,t_0)</math> and dropped <math>t_0</math> for compactness.

'''Step 3.''' We now substitute <math>\xi = \gamma</math> and <math>\delta\xi = \delta\gamma</math> into the expression for <math>\delta\mathcal{S}_{\delta \xi}[\xi,t;t_0]</math> from Step 1 and compare the result with the formula derived in Step 2. The fact that, for <math>t > t_0,</math> the vector field <math>\delta \gamma</math> was chosen arbitrarily completes the proof.
}}

=== Formula ===
Given the [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian]] <math>H(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{p},t)</math> of a mechanical system, the Hamilton–Jacobi equation is a first-order, [[non-linear differential equation|non-linear]] [[partial differential equation]] for the Hamilton's principal function <math>S</math>,<ref>{{cite book |first1=L. N. |last1=Hand |first2=J. D. |last2=Finch |title=Analytical Mechanics |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-521-57572-0 }}</ref>

{{Equation box 1
|equation = <math> - \frac{\partial S}{\partial t} = H{\left(\mathbf{q},\frac{\partial S}{\partial \mathbf{q}},t \right)}.</math>
|2=border|border colour = #50C878
|background colour = #ECFCF4|title=}}

{{math proof | title = Derivation | proof =
For an extremal <math>\xi=\xi(t;t_0,\mathbf{q}_0,\mathbf{v}_0),</math> where <math>\mathbf{v}_0 = \dot\xi|_{t=t_0}</math> is the initial speed (see discussion preceding the definition of HPF),
<math display="block">
\mathcal{L}(\xi(t),\dot\xi(t),t)
= \frac{dS(\xi(t),t)}{dt}
= \left[\frac{\partial S}{\partial \mathbf{q}}\mathbf{\dot q} + \frac{\partial S}{\partial t}\right]^{\mathbf{q}=\xi(t)}_{\mathbf{\dot q} = \dot\xi(t)}.
</math>

From the formula for <math>p_i = p_i(\mathbf{q}, t)</math> and the coordinate-based definition of the Hamiltonian
<math display="block">H(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{p},t) = \mathbf{p}\mathbf{\dot q} - \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{\dot q},t),</math>
with <math>\mathbf{\dot q}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q},t)</math> satisfying the (uniquely solvable for <math>\mathbf{\dot q})</math> equation <math display="inline"> \mathbf{p} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{\dot q},t)}{\partial \mathbf{\dot q}},</math> obtain
<math display="block">
\frac{\partial S}{\partial t} = \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{\dot q},t) - \frac{\partial S}{\mathbf{\partial q}}\mathbf{\dot q} = -H{\left(\mathbf{q},\frac{\partial S}{\partial \mathbf{q}},t\right)},
</math>
where <math>\mathbf{q} = \xi(t)</math> and <math>\mathbf{\dot q} = \dot\xi(t).</math>
}}

Alternatively, as described below, the Hamilton–Jacobi equation may be derived from [[Hamiltonian mechanics]] by treating <math> S</math> as the [[generating function (physics)|generating function]] for a [[canonical transformation]] of the classical Hamiltonian
<math display="block">H = H(q_1,q_2,\ldots, q_N;p_1,p_2,\ldots, p_N;t).</math>

The conjugate momenta correspond to the first derivatives of <math>S</math> with respect to the generalized coordinates
<math display="block">p_k = \frac{\partial S}{\partial q_k}.</math>

As a solution to the Hamilton–Jacobi equation, the principal function contains <math>N+1</math> undetermined constants, the first <math>N</math> of them denoted as <math>\alpha_1,\, \alpha_2, \dots , \alpha_N</math>, and the last one coming from the integration of <math>\frac{\partial S}{\partial t}</math>.

The relationship between <math>\mathbf{p}</math> and <math>\mathbf{q}</math> then describes the orbit in [[phase space]] in terms of these [[constants of motion]]. Furthermore, the quantities
<math display="block">\beta_k=\frac{\partial S}{\partial\alpha_k},\quad k=1,2, \ldots, N </math>
are also constants of motion, and these equations can be inverted to find <math>\mathbf{q}</math> as a function of all the <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> constants and time.<ref name=Goldstein_440>{{cite book |last=Goldstein |first=Herbert |author-link=Herbert Goldstein |year=1980 |title= Classical Mechanics |edition=2nd |publisher=Addison-Wesley |location=Reading, MA |isbn= 978-0-201-02918-5 |page=440|title-link=Classical Mechanics (Goldstein) }}</ref>

== Comparison with other formulations of mechanics ==

The Hamilton–Jacobi equation is a ''single'', first-order partial differential equation for the function  of the <math>N</math> [[generalized coordinate]]s <math>q_1,\, q_2, \dots , q_N</math> and the time <math>t</math>. The generalized momenta do not appear, except as derivatives of <math>S</math>, the [[Action (physics)|classical action]].

For comparison, in the equivalent [[Euler–Lagrange equation|Euler–Lagrange equations of motion]] of [[Lagrangian mechanics]], the conjugate momenta also do not appear; however, those equations are a ''system'' of <math>N</math>, generally second-order equations for the time evolution of the generalized coordinates. Similarly, [[Hamilton's equations|Hamilton's equations of motion]] are another ''system'' of 2''N'' first-order equations for the time evolution of the generalized coordinates and their conjugate momenta <math>p_1,\, p_2, \dots , p_N</math>.

Since the HJE is an equivalent expression of an integral minimization problem such as [[Hamilton's principle]], the HJE can be useful in other problems of the [[calculus of variations]] and, more generally,  in other branches of [[mathematics]] and [[physics]], such as [[dynamical systems]], [[symplectic geometry]] and [[quantum chaos]].  For example, the Hamilton–Jacobi equations can be used to determine the [[geodesic]]s on a [[Riemannian manifold]], an important [[calculus of variations|variational problem]] in [[Riemannian geometry]]. However as a computational tool, the partial differential equations are notoriously complicated to solve except when is it possible to separate the independent variables; in this case the HJE become computationally useful.<ref name=Goldstein3>{{Cite book |last=Goldstein |first=Herbert |title=Classical mechanics |last2=Poole |first2=Charles P. |last3=Safko |first3=John L. |date=2008 |publisher=Addison Wesley |isbn=978-0-201-65702-9 |edition=3, [Nachdr.] |location=San Francisco Munich |title-link=Classical Mechanics (Goldstein)}}</ref>{{rp|444}}

== Derivation using a canonical transformation ==
Any [[canonical transformation]] involving a type-2 [[generating function (physics)|generating function]] <math>G_2 (\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{P}, t)</math> leads to the relations
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
&\mathbf{p} = \frac{\partial G_2}{\partial \mathbf{q}}, \quad
 \mathbf{Q} = \frac{\partial G_2}{\partial \mathbf{P}}, \quad \\
&K(\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{P},t) = H(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{p},t) + \frac{\partial G_2}{\partial t}
\end{align}
</math>
and Hamilton's equations in terms of the new variables <math>\mathbf{P}, \,\mathbf{Q}</math> and new Hamiltonian <math>K</math> have the same form:
<math display="block"> \dot{\mathbf{P}}  = -{\partial K \over \partial \mathbf{Q}},
\quad \dot{\mathbf{Q}}  = +{\partial K \over \partial \mathbf{P}}. </math>

To derive the HJE, a generating function <math>G_2 (\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{P}, t)</math> is chosen in such a way that, it will make the new Hamiltonian <math>K=0</math>. Hence, all its derivatives are also zero, and the transformed Hamilton's equations become trivial
<math display="block">\dot{\mathbf{P}} = \dot{\mathbf{Q}} = 0</math>
so the new generalized coordinates and momenta are [[constant of motion|''constants'' of motion]].  As they are constants, in this context the new generalized momenta <math>\mathbf{P}</math> are usually denoted <math>\alpha_1,\, \alpha_2, \dots , \alpha_N</math>, i.e. <math>P_m =\alpha_m</math> and the new [[generalized coordinates]] <math>\mathbf{Q}</math> are typically denoted as <math>\beta_1,\, \beta_2, \dots , \beta_N</math>, so <math>Q_m =\beta_m</math>.

Setting the generating function equal to Hamilton's principal function, plus an arbitrary constant <math>A</math>:
<math display="block">G_2(\mathbf{q},\boldsymbol{\alpha},t)=S(\mathbf{q},t)+A, </math>
the HJE automatically arises
<math display="block">\begin{align}
& \mathbf{p} = \frac{\partial G_2}{\partial \mathbf{q}}=\frac{\partial S}{\partial \mathbf{q}} \\[1ex]
\rightarrow {} &
H(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{p},t) + {\partial G_2 \over \partial t}=0 \\[1ex]
\rightarrow {} &
H{\left(\mathbf{q},\frac{\partial S}{\partial \mathbf{q}},t\right)} + {\partial S \over \partial t} = 0.
\end{align}</math>

When solved for <math> S(\mathbf{q},\boldsymbol\alpha, t) </math>, these also give us the useful equations
<math display="block">\mathbf{Q} = \boldsymbol\beta = {\partial S \over \partial \boldsymbol\alpha},</math>
or written in components for clarity
<math display="block"> Q_m = \beta_m =  \frac{\partial S(\mathbf{q},\boldsymbol\alpha, t)}{\partial \alpha_m}. </math>

Ideally, these {{mvar|N}} equations can be inverted to find the original [[generalized coordinates]] <math> \mathbf{q} </math> as a function of the constants <math> \boldsymbol\alpha, \,\boldsymbol\beta, </math> and <math> t </math>, thus solving the original problem.

== Separation of variables ==
When the problem allows [[separation of variables|additive separation of variables]], the HJE leads directly to [[constant of motion|constants of motion]].  For example, the time ''t'' can be separated if the Hamiltonian does not depend on time explicitly.  In that case, the time derivative <math>\frac{\partial S}{\partial t} </math> in the HJE must be a constant, usually denoted (<math>-E </math>), giving the separated solution
<math display="block"> S = W(q_1,q_2, \ldots, q_N) - Et </math>
where the time-independent function <math>W(\mathbf{q}) </math> is sometimes called the '''abbreviated action''' or '''Hamilton's characteristic function''' <ref name=Goldstein3/>{{rp|434}} and sometimes<ref name=HancTaylorTuleja>{{Cite journal |last1=Hanc |first1=Jozef |last2=Taylor |first2=Edwin F. |last3=Tuleja |first3=Slavomir |date=2005-07-01 |title=Variational mechanics in one and two dimensions |url=https://pubs.aip.org/ajp/article/73/7/603/1056166/Variational-mechanics-in-one-and-two-dimensions |journal=American Journal of Physics |language=en |volume=73 |issue=7 |pages=603–610 |doi=10.1119/1.1848516 |bibcode=2005AmJPh..73..603H |issn=0002-9505|url-access=subscription }}</ref>{{rp|607}}  written <math>S_0</math> (see [[history of variational principles in physics#action principle names|action principle names]]). The reduced Hamilton–Jacobi equation can then be written
<math display="block"> H{\left(\mathbf{q},\frac{\partial S}{\partial \mathbf{q}} \right)} = E. </math>

To illustrate separability for other variables, a certain [[generalized coordinate]] <math>q_k </math> and its derivative <math>\frac{\partial S}{\partial q_k} </math> are assumed to appear together as a single function
<math display="block">\psi{\left(q_k, \frac{\partial S}{\partial q_k} \right)}</math>
in the Hamiltonian
<math display="block"> H = H(q_1,q_2,\ldots, q_{k-1}, q_{k+1},\ldots, q_N; p_1,p_2,\ldots, p_{k-1}, p_{k+1},\ldots, p_N; \psi; t). </math>

In that case, the function ''S'' can be partitioned into two functions, one that depends only on ''q<sub>k</sub>'' and another that depends only on the remaining [[generalized coordinate]]s
<math display="block">S = S_k(q_k) + S_\text{rem}(q_1,\ldots, q_{k-1}, q_{k+1}, \ldots, q_N, t). </math>

Substitution of these formulae into the Hamilton–Jacobi equation shows that the function ''ψ'' must be a constant (denoted here as <math>\Gamma_k </math>), yielding a first-order [[ordinary differential equation]] for <math>S_k (q_k), </math>

<math display="block"> \psi{\left(q_k, \frac{ d S_k}{ d q_k} \right)} = \Gamma_k. </math>

In fortunate cases, the function <math>S </math> can be separated completely into <math>N </math> functions <math>S_m (q_m), </math>
<math display="block"> S=S_1(q_1)+S_2(q_2)+\cdots+S_N(q_N)-Et. </math>

In such a case, the problem devolves to <math>N </math> [[ordinary differential equation]]s.

The separability of ''S'' depends both on the Hamiltonian and on the choice of [[generalized coordinate]]s.  For [[orthogonal coordinates]] and Hamiltonians that have no time dependence and are [[Quadratic function|quadratic]] in the generalized momenta, <math>S </math> will be completely separable if the potential energy is additively separable in each coordinate, where the potential energy term for each coordinate is multiplied by the coordinate-dependent factor in the corresponding momentum term of the Hamiltonian (the '''Staeckel conditions''').  For illustration, several examples in [[orthogonal coordinates]] are worked in the next sections.

=== Separation in spherical coordinates ===
{{Further|Coordinate system|Orthogonal coordinates|Curvilinear coordinates}}
In [[spherical coordinates]] the Hamiltonian of a free particle moving in a conservative potential ''U'' can be written<ref name=Landau-v1>{{Cite book |last=Landau |first=Lev Davidovič |title=Mechanics |last2=Lifšic |first2=Evgenij M. |last3=Landau |first3=Lev Davidovič |last4=Landau |first4=Lev Davidovič |date=2011 |publisher=Elsevier, Butterworth-Heinemann |isbn=978-0-7506-2896-9 |edition=3. ed., repr |series=Course of theoretical physics / L. D. Landau and E. M. Lifshitz |location=Amsterdam Heidelberg}}</ref>{{rp|151}}
<math display="block"> H = \frac{1}{2m} \left[ p_r^2 + \frac{p_{\theta}^2}{r^2} + \frac{p_{\phi}^2}{r^2 \sin^2 \theta} \right] + U(r, \theta, \phi). </math>

The Hamilton–Jacobi equation is separable in these coordinates provided that there exist functions <math> U_r(r), U_{\theta}(\theta), U_{\phi}(\phi) </math> such that <math>U</math> can be written in the analogous form
<math display="block"> U(r, \theta, \phi) = U_r(r) + \frac{U_{\theta}(\theta)}{r^2} + \frac{U_{\phi}(\phi)}{r^2\sin^2\theta} . </math>

The last term has few physical applications.
Dropping that term, the HJE becomes
<math display="block">
\frac{1}{2m} \left( \frac{ dS_r}{ dr} \right)^2 + U_r(r) +
\frac{1}{2m r^2} \left[ \left( \frac{ dS_{\theta}}{ d\theta} \right)^2 + 2m U_{\theta}(\theta) \right] +
\frac{1}{2m r^2\sin^2\theta} \left( \frac{ dS_{\phi}}{ d\phi} \right)^2 = E.
</math>
The <math>\phi</math> coordinate is ''cyclic''<ref name=Landau-v1/>{{rp|150}} and the solution can be written in the form
<math> S_0 = p_\phi + S_r(r) + S_\theta(\theta),</math>
resulting in two [[ordinary differential equation]]s for the remaining coordinates:
<math display="block"> \left(  \frac{ dS_{\theta}}{ d\theta} \right)^2 +  2m  U_{\theta}(\theta) +  \frac{p_{\phi}}{\sin^2\theta} = \Gamma_{\theta} </math>
<math display="block"> \frac{1}{2m} \left( \frac{dS_r}{ dr} \right)^2 + U_r(r) + \frac{\Gamma_{\theta}}{2m r^2} = E </math>
where <math>p_\phi</math>, <math>\Gamma_\theta</math>, and <math>E</math> are [[constant of motion|constants of the motion]]. This reduces the HJE to the [[ordinary differential equation]]s whose integration completes the solution for <math>S</math>.

== Waves and particles ==

=== Optical wave fronts and trajectories ===
{{Main |Hamilton's optico-mechanical analogy}}
The HJE establishes a duality between trajectories and [[wavefront]]s.<ref>{{cite journal| last1=Houchmandzadeh| first1=Bahram| date=2020| title=The Hamilton-Jacobi Equation: an alternative approach| url=https://aapt.scitation.org/doi/10.1119/10.0000781| journal=American Journal of Physics| volume=85| issue=5| article-number=10.1119/10.0000781| doi=10.1119/10.0000781| ref=houchmandzadeh2020| arxiv=1910.09414| bibcode=2020AmJPh..88..353H| s2cid=204800598}}</ref> For example, in geometrical optics, light can be considered either as "rays" or waves. The wave front can be defined as the surface <math display="inline">\mathcal{C}_t</math> that the light emitted at time <math display="inline">t=0</math> has reached at time <math display="inline">t</math>. Light rays and wave fronts are dual: if one is known, the other can be deduced.

More precisely, geometrical optics is a variational problem where the "action" is the travel time <math display="inline">T</math> along a path,<math display="block">T = \frac{1}{c} \int_A^B n \, ds</math> where <math display="inline">n</math> is the medium's [[Refractive index|index of refraction]] and <math display="inline">ds</math> is an infinitesimal arc length. From the above formulation, one can compute the ray paths using the Euler–Lagrange formulation; alternatively, one can compute the wave fronts by solving the Hamilton–Jacobi equation. Knowing one leads to knowing the other.

The above duality is very general and applies to ''all'' systems that derive from a variational principle: either compute the trajectories using Euler–Lagrange equations or the wave fronts by using Hamilton–Jacobi equation.

The wave front at time <math display="inline">t</math>, for a system initially at <math display="inline">\mathbf{q}_0</math> at time <math display="inline">t_0</math>, is defined as the collection of points <math display="inline">\mathbf{q}</math> such that <math display="inline">S(\mathbf{q},t) = \text{const}</math>. If <math display="inline">S(\mathbf{q},t)</math> is known, the momentum is immediately deduced.
<math display="block">\mathbf{p}=\frac{\partial S}{\partial\mathbf{q}}.</math>

Once <math display="inline">\mathbf{p}</math> is known, tangents to the trajectories <math display="inline">\dot{\mathbf{q}}</math> are computed by solving the equation<math display="block">\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\dot{ \mathbf{q}}}=\boldsymbol{p}</math>for <math display="inline">\dot{\mathbf{q}}</math>, where <math display="inline">\mathcal{L}</math> is the Lagrangian. The trajectories are then recovered from the knowledge of <math display="inline">\dot{\mathbf{q}}</math>.

=== Relationship to the Schrödinger equation ===
{{Further|Eikonal approximation}}
The [[isosurface]]s of the function <math>S(\mathbf{q}, t)</math> can be determined at any time ''t''.  The motion of an <math>S</math>-isosurface as a function of time is defined by the motions of the particles beginning at the points <math>\mathbf{q}</math> on the isosurface.  The motion of such an isosurface can be thought of as a ''[[wave]]'' moving through <math>\mathbf{q}</math>-space, although it does not obey the [[wave equation]] exactly.  To show this, let ''S'' represent the [[phase (waves)|phase]] of a wave
<math display="block"> \psi = \psi_0 e^{iS/\hbar} </math>
where <math>\hbar</math> is a constant (the [[Planck constant]]) introduced to make the exponential argument dimensionless, and <math>\psi_0</math> is a scalar normalization constant; changes in the [[amplitude]] of the [[wave]] can be represented by having <math>S</math> be a [[complex number]].

The [[Schrödinger equation]] is :<math display="block"> \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 \psi - U\psi = \frac{\hbar}{i} \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial t} </math>

Starting with the Schrödinger equation and our [[ansatz]] for <math>\psi</math>, it can be deduced that<ref name="Goldstein_490">{{cite book |last=Goldstein |first=Herbert |author-link=Herbert Goldstein |year=1980 |title= Classical Mechanics |edition=2nd |publisher=Addison-Wesley |location=Reading, MA | isbn= 978-0-201-02918-5 | pages=490–491| title-link=Classical Mechanics (Goldstein) }}</ref>
<math display="block"> \frac{1}{2m} \left( \nabla S \right)^2 + U + \frac{\partial S}{\partial t} = \frac{i\hbar}{2m} \nabla^2 S.</math> This is the Schrödinger equation in nonlinear [[Riccati equation|Riccati]] form<ref name="Mustafa_2025">{{cite journal |last1=Türe |first1=Mustafa |last2=Ünsal |first2=Mithat |date=May 12, 2025 |title=Quantum Hamilton-Jacobi theory, spectral path integrals, and exact WKB analysis |journal=Physical Review D |volume=111 |issue=10 |article-number=105010 |publisher=American Physical Society |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.111.105010 |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevD.111.105010}}</ref>.

The classical limit (<math>\hbar \rightarrow 0</math>) of the Schrödinger equation above becomes identical to the following variant of the Hamilton–Jacobi equation,
<math display="block"> \frac{1}{2m} \left( \nabla S \right)^2 + U + \frac{\partial S}{\partial t} = 0. </math>

The following table summarizes the similarities between optics and quantum mechancis.
The Hamilton-Jacobi equation is to quantum mechanics what the [[eikonal equation]] is to the [[Helmholtz equation|wave equation of optics]]. Both the eikonal equation and the Hamilton-Jacobi equation are slowly varying approximations ([[WKB approximation|WKB approximations]]) of the corresponding more fundamental wave equations.

<div style="display:flex; justify-content:space-around; text-align:center;">

<!-- Optics column -->
<div style="flex:1;">
<b>Optics</b><br/><br/>
<math>\nabla^2 \psi - \frac{1}{c^2(x)} \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial t^2} = 0</math><br/>
<small>[[Electromagnetic wave equation|EM Wave equation]]</small><br/>
&nbsp;&darr;<br/>
<math>-\frac{n(\partial_t S)^2}{c^2} + \frac{(\nabla S)^2}{n} + (mc)^2 = 0</math><br/>
<small>Time dependant eikonal equation</small><br/>
&nbsp;&darr;<br/>
<math>|\nabla S(x)|^2 = n^2(x)</math><br/>
<small>[[Eikonal equation]]</small><br/>

</div>

<!-- Quantum mechanics column -->
<div style="flex:1;">
<b>Quantum mechanics</b><br/><br/>
<math>i \hbar \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial t} = \hat{H} \psi</math><br/>
<small>[[Schrödinger equation]]</small><br/>
&nbsp;&darr;<br/>
<math>\partial_t S + H(x,\nabla S,t) = 0</math><br/>
<small>[[Hamilton–Jacobi equation]]</small><br/>
</div>

</div>

== Applications ==

=== HJE in a gravitational field ===

Using the [[energy–momentum relation]] in the form<ref>{{cite book|author1=Wheeler|first=John|title=Gravitation|title-link=Gravitation (book)|last2=Misner|first2=Charles|last3=Thorne|first3=Kip|publisher=W.H. Freeman & Co|year=1973|isbn=978-0-7167-0344-0|pages=649, 1188}}</ref>
<math display="block">g^{\alpha\beta}P_\alpha P_\beta - (mc)^2 = 0 </math>
for a particle of [[rest mass]] <math>m </math> travelling in curved space, where <math>g^{\alpha \beta}</math> are the [[Covariance and contravariance of vectors|contravariant]] coordinates of the [[metric tensor]] (i.e., the [[Metric tensor#Inverse metric|inverse metric]]) solved from the [[Einstein field equations]], and <math>c</math> is the [[speed of light]]. Setting the [[four-momentum]] <math>P_\alpha</math> equal to the [[four-gradient]] of the action <math>S </math>,
<math display="block">P_\alpha =-\frac{\partial S}{\partial x^\alpha}</math>
gives the Hamilton–Jacobi equation in the geometry determined by the metric <math>g </math>:
<math display="block">g^{\alpha\beta}\frac{\partial S}{\partial x^\alpha}\frac{\partial S}{\partial x^\beta} -(mc)^2 = 0,</math>
in other words, in a [[gravitational field]].

=== HJE in electromagnetic fields ===

For a particle of [[rest mass]] <math>m</math> and electric charge <math>e</math>  moving in electromagnetic field with [[four-potential]]  <math>A_i  =  (\phi,\Alpha)</math> in vacuum, the Hamilton–Jacobi equation in geometry determined by the metric tensor <math>g^{ik} = g_{ik}</math> has a form
<math display="block">g^{ik}\left ( \frac{\partial S}{\partial x^i} + \frac {e}{c}A_i \right ) \left ( \frac{\partial S}{\partial x^k} + \frac {e}{c}A_k \right ) = m^2 c^2</math>
and can be solved for the Hamilton principal action function <math>S</math> to obtain further solution for the particle trajectory and momentum:<ref>{{cite book |title=The Classical Theory of Fields |first1=L. |last1=Landau |author-link=Lev Landau |first2=E. |last2=Lifshitz |author-link2=Evgeny Lifshitz |publisher=Addison-Wesley |location=Reading, Massachusetts |year=1959 |oclc=17966515 }}</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
x &= - \frac {e}{c \gamma}\int A_z \,d\xi, &
y &= - \frac {e}{c \gamma} \int A_y \,d\xi, \\[1ex]
z &= - \frac {e^2}{2c^2 \gamma^2} \int \left(\Alpha^2 - \overline {\Alpha^2 }\right) \, d\xi, &
\xi &= ct - \frac{e^2}{2 \gamma^2 c^2} \int \left(\Alpha^2 - \overline {\Alpha^2}\right)  \, d\xi, \\[1ex]
p_x &= - \frac{e}{c} A_x, &
p_y &= - \frac{e}{c} A_y, \\[1ex]
p_z &= \frac{e^2}{2\gamma c} \left(\Alpha^2 - \overline {\Alpha^2}\right), &
\mathcal{E} &= c\gamma + \frac{e^2}{2 \gamma c} \left(\Alpha^2 - \overline {\Alpha^2}\right),
\end{align}</math>
where <math>\xi = ct - z</math> and <math>\gamma^2 = m^2 c^2 + \frac{e^2}{c^2} \overline{A}^2 </math> with <math>\overline{\mathbf{A}}</math> the cycle average of the vector potential.

==== A circularly polarized wave ====
In the case of [[circular polarization]],
<math display="block">\begin{align}
E_x &= E_0 \sin \omega \xi_1, &
E_y &= E_0 \cos \omega \xi_1, \\[1ex]
A_x &= \frac{ cE_0 }{\omega} \cos \omega \xi_1, &
A_y &= - \frac{ cE_0 }{\omega} \sin \omega \xi_1.
\end{align} </math>

Hence
<math display="block">\begin{align}
x &= - \frac{ecE_0} \omega \sin \omega \xi_1, &
y &= - \frac{ecE_0} \omega \cos \omega \xi_1, \\[1ex]
p_x &= - \frac{eE_0} \omega \cos \omega \xi_1, &
p_y &= \frac{eE_0}{\omega} \sin \omega \xi_1,
\end{align}</math>

where <math>\xi_1 = \xi /c </math>, implying the particle moving along a circular trajectory with a permanent radius <math>e cE_0 / \gamma \omega^2 </math> and an invariable value of momentum <math>e E_0 / \omega^2 </math> directed along a magnetic field vector.

==== A monochromatic linearly polarized plane wave ====
For the flat, monochromatic, linearly polarized wave with a field <math>E</math> directed along the axis <math>y</math>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
E_y &= E_0 \cos \omega \xi_1, &
A_y &= - \frac {cE_0}{\omega} \sin \omega \xi_1,
\end{align}</math>
hence
<math display="block">\begin{align}
x &= \text{const}, \\[1ex]
y &= y_0 \cos \omega \xi_1, &
y_0 &= -\frac{ecE_0}{\gamma \omega^2}, \\[1ex]
z &= C_z y_0 \sin 2\omega \xi_1, &
C_z &= \frac{eE_0}{8\gamma \omega}, \\[1ex]
\gamma^2 &= m^2 c^2  + \frac{e^2 E_0^2}{2 \omega^2},
\end{align}</math><math display="block">\begin{align}
p_x &= 0, \\[1ex]
p_y &= p_{y,0} \sin \omega \xi_1, &
p_{y,0} &= \frac{eE_0}{\omega}, \\[1ex]
p_z &= - 2C_z p_{y,0} \cos 2\omega \xi_1
\end{align}</math>

implying the particle figure-8 trajectory with its axis oriented along the electric field <math>E</math> vector.

==== An electromagnetic wave with a solenoidal magnetic field ====
For the electromagnetic wave with axial (solenoidal) magnetic field:<ref>{{cite journal|title=Inductively Coupling Plasma Reactor With Plasma Electron Energy Controllable in the Range from ~6 to ~100 eV|journal=IEEE Transactions on Plasma Science |author1=E. V. Shun'ko |author2=D. E. Stevenson |author3=V. S. Belkin |volume= 42, part II|issue= 3|pages= 774–785|doi=10.1109/TPS.2014.2299954|bibcode = 2014ITPS...42..774S |year=2014 |s2cid=34765246 }}</ref>
<math display="block">E = E_\phi = \frac{\omega \rho_0}{c} B_0 \cos \omega \xi_1, </math>
<math display="block">A_\phi = - \rho_0 B_0 \sin \omega \xi_1 =  - \frac{L_s}{\pi \rho_0 N_s} I_0 \sin \omega \xi_1,</math>
hence
<math display="block">\begin{align}
x &= \text{constant}, \\
y &= y_0 \cos \omega \xi_1, &
y_0 &= -\frac{e \rho_0 B_0}{\gamma \omega}, \\
z &= C_z y_0 \sin 2\omega \xi_1, &
C_z &= \frac{e \rho_0 B_0}{8c \gamma}, \\
\gamma^2 &= m^2 c^2 + \frac{e^2 \rho_0^2 B_0^2}{2c^2},
\end{align}</math>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
p_x &= 0, \\
p_y &= p_{y,0} \sin \omega \xi_1, &
p_{y,0} &= \frac{e \rho_0 B_0}{c}, \\
p_z &= - 2C_z p_{y,0} \cos 2 \omega \xi_1,
\end{align}</math>
where <math>B_0</math> is the magnetic field magnitude in a solenoid with the effective radius <math>\rho_0</math>, inductivity <math>L_s</math>, number of windings <math>N_s</math>, and an electric current magnitude <math>I_0</math> through the solenoid windings. The particle motion occurs along the figure-8 trajectory in <math>yz</math> plane set perpendicular to the solenoid axis with arbitrary azimuth angle <math>\varphi</math> due to axial symmetry of the solenoidal magnetic field.
